Benchmark-quality measures: line and branch coverage of the test suites per level and language (overall line coverage 79.7% → 93.9% after supplementation); LLM-panel input-quality score (completeness, clarity, consistency, implementability; threshold > 3.5). Qualitative failure analysis (e.g. Claude Code non-termination at L2)

Automatic: generated artefacts frozen and reintegrated into Oracle-derived repositories, built and tested in Docker with each repository's native workflow (pytest, JUnit5, go test, Google Test, Jest); L0/L1 run interface-level functional tests, L2/L3 the associated tests; coverage with pytest-cov, JaCoCo, go test -coverprofile, lcov, Jest/nyc; tokens and cost from API usage. Tests supplemented by Claude Sonnet 4.6 for under-covered repositories. Statistics: two-sided exact McNemar (Build, Full) and Wilcoxon signed-rank (Test), Holm correction, α = 0.05. Manual: sampled failure inspection

Tasks: 2,590 PolyCodeEval tasks, all levels derived from the same 58 Oracle repositories. Configurations: per level (L0: Claude Code, Codex, ChatDev × 2 LLMs; L1: Claude Code, Codex; L2: agents vs direct generation with the same backbone; L3: 4 methods × 3 LLMs). Baselines: direct LLM generation (L2, L3), ChatDev (L0). Held constant: tasks, inputs, Docker environments, dependencies, build and test commands, integration procedure; same backbone per method at L3; agents' internal sampling not matched to direct generation; temperature 0.2 for direct calls; retries only for infrastructure failures. Acceptance tests: native plus LLM-supplemented test suites (all repositories > 85% line coverage), every task validated with the Oracle implementation. Repetitions: one run (not stated otherwise). Human intervention: none. RQ4: paired comparisons L0 vs L1 and L2-to-L3 vs L3 Direct (1,891 shared tasks)

L0: Claude Code best (Full 22.4%) over Codex (20.7%) and ChatDev (17.2%, 12.1%); Codex cheaper than Claude Code ($14.87 vs $48.76); no significance test reported for L0/L1. L1: skeleton raises Full (+8.6 pp for both agents) and Test but lowers Build (Claude Code 74.1 → 62.1, Codex 63.8 → 60.3) and raises cost. L2: Codex vs Direct GPT +17.3 pp Build (significant, McNemar Holm-adjusted p = 3.08×10⁻⁵) and +21.4 pp Full; Claude Code vs Direct Sonnet no significant Build difference (Full 56.7 vs 57.3). L3: RepoCoder and HCP with GPT significantly better than Direct on Build, Test and Full (p < 3.3×10⁻⁷); AlignCoder only on Build (p = 6.0×10⁻⁴); RepoCoder-GPT best (Full 71.7%) and significantly above AlignCoder-GPT (all metrics) and HCP-GPT (Build, Full), but uses 10.4× the tokens of Direct. RQ4: related implementation context raises function Full from 50.1% to 55.0% (GPT-5.4, p = 5.31×10⁻⁴) and from 40.2% to 51.6% (Sonnet 4.6, p = 2.24×10⁻¹⁴). Large variation across languages at every level

Partly: the execution-based protocol separated methods and levels, with paired significance tests at L2, L3 and RQ4; rankings changed across granularities and languages, which the authors present as the reason for multi-granularity evaluation. Not shown to be repeatable (single run, no repetitions); L0/L1 differences not tested. Limitations stated: repository selection (mature open-source projects), LLM-generated task descriptions, possible training-data contamination

Threats: findings may not generalise to private, legacy or other repositories; task descriptions generated by Claude Sonnet 4.6 may not fully capture intended functionality (mitigated by a three-LLM review and manual revision); contamination and memorisation cannot be excluded, so results are not contamination-free generalisation estimates. Gaps: existing methods perform poorly (at most 71.7% functions, 76.7% files, 31.0% repositories fully correct); repository-level generation needs stronger engineering integration (build, dependencies, interfaces); file-level needs better interface and dependency understanding; function-level needs better context selection; cost and effectiveness trade off

Data availability: benchmark, configurations, prompts, scripts, evaluation results and statistics released at https://polycodeeval.github.io/PolyCodeEval. No pre-registration. Languages: Python, JavaScript, Java, Go, C++. Inconsistencies/caveats: the introduction says the skeleton 'does not yield a consistent overall improvement', while RQ4 reports Full gains for both agents (with lower Build); Table 5 and 6 token and cost columns are garbled in the text extraction, so the L2 token/cost mapping and all L3 costs need checking in the PDF (L3 Build/Test/Full values agree with the text); the supplementary tests and all task specifications were generated by Claude Sonnet 4.6, one of the evaluated models; Claude Code produced no evaluable output on 20 of 150 L2 tasks (time limit 10 min). Experiments on a local laptop (Intel Core i9, RTX 4070 Laptop GPU, 16 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04) with models via APIs
